Scaling the gold standard from 72 to 300+ claims

LLM pre-annotation (Gemma 4) + human review (Shiny)

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/llm-annotation-workflow.Rmd
llm-annotation-workflow.Rmd

Why scale the gold standard

The extraction benchmark (vignette("llm-kg-benchmark")) runs on 30 synthetic abstracts × 72 claims – enough to validate the infrastructure, not enough for a paper. With 300 claims annotated on real abstracts from OpenAlex / SciELO:

  • The 95% Wilson confidence interval on F1 narrows from [0.69, 0.88] to [0.75, 0.84] – narrow enough to declare differences between backends.
  • With subgroups by topic (management, climate, texture, …) each cell holds at least 30 claims, the statistical minimum for subgroup analysis.
  • Claims in real abstracts expose each LLM’s idiosyncrasies with real pedological jargon (Latin names of grass species, WRB acronyms, etc.).

Annotating 300 claims from scratch would take a pedologist about two days. This tool cuts that to about three hours through pre-annotation plus review.

The three-step workflow 

┌────────────────────────┐
│  corpus.jsonl          │   (fetched from OpenAlex/SciELO)
│  abstracts only        │
└───────────┬────────────┘
            │  llm_preannotate()
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  draft_gold.jsonl      │   (Gemma 4 extractions, status="draft")
└───────────┬────────────┘
            │  llm_annotation_launch()
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  reviewed.jsonl        │   (human accept / edit / reject / add)
└───────────┬────────────┘
            │  llm_annotation_export()
            ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  gold_v2_final.jsonl   │   (publication-grade, drafts removed)
└────────────────────────┘

Step 1 – Build the corpus

Option A (production): fetch 100-300 real abstracts on Cerrado pedogenesis from OpenAlex:

library(edaphos)

# OpenAlex -- orthogonal queries to cover the domain
queries <- c(
  "cerrado AND (pedogenesis OR soil formation)",
  "cerrado AND soil organic carbon",
  "(cerrado OR savanna) AND (clay OR texture) AND soil",
  "cerrado AND (land use change OR deforestation) AND soil"
)
corpus_list <- lapply(queries, function(q) {
  causal_corpus_openalex(q, max_results = 50L)
})
corpus <- do.call(rbind, corpus_list)
corpus <- causal_corpus_deduplicate(corpus)   # drop DOI duplicates
nrow(corpus)  # ~180-200 unique abstracts

# Convert to the schema the pre-annotator expects
corpus_records <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(corpus)), function(i) {
  list(
    abstract_id   = paste0("OA_", sprintf("%04d", i)),
    title         = corpus$title[i],
    abstract_text = corpus$abstract[i],
    year          = corpus$year[i],
    doi           = corpus$doi[i]
  )
})
# Write JSONL
con <- file("cerrado_corpus_openalex_2026.jsonl", "w")
for (r in corpus_records) writeLines(
  jsonlite::toJSON(r, auto_unbox = TRUE), con)
close(con)

Option B (demo): use the 30 synthetic abstracts already shipped:

# Produces inst/extdata/cerrado_gold_standard_v1_draft.jsonl
source("data-raw/annotation_tool_demo.R")

Step 2 – Pre-annotation with Gemma 4

llm_preannotate() reads the corpus and writes a draft in which every claim has status = "draft", so the reviewer knows it came from the LLM and not from a person:

llm_preannotate(
  corpus      = "cerrado_corpus_openalex_2026.jsonl",
  backend     = "ollama",          # local, free
  model       = "gemma4:latest",
  output_path = "draft_gold_v2.jsonl",
  cache_dir   = "~/.cache/edaphos_annotation",
  verbose     = TRUE
)

With Ollama running and gemma4:latest pulled, 100 abstracts take about 25 minutes. cache_dir makes the run resume-safe – if the process dies, re-run it and it skips the cache hits.

No Ollama? Use the deterministic fallback:

llm_preannotate(corpus, backend = "simulator",
                 output_path = "draft_gold_v2.jsonl")

The simulator does not understand the abstracts – it only samples vocabulary-to-vocabulary pairs – but it produces a draft in a valid schema, useful for testing the review tool.

Step 3 – Human review (Shiny)

This is the three-hour part. Open the reviewer:

llm_annotation_launch(
  draft_path         = "draft_gold_v2.jsonl",
  output_path        = "reviewed_gold_v2.jsonl",
  keyboard_shortcuts = TRUE
)

The app opens in your default browser. The interface has three tabs.

Tab 1 – Review

  • Header: abstract ID + title + metadata + the full abstract text in a highlighted box.
  • Claims table: each claim takes one row, with editable dropdowns for cause / effect (restricted to the canonical vocabulary), a radio button for polarity, a slider for confidence, a text field for rationale, and two buttons: ✓ Accept ✗ Reject.
  • Navigation buttons: “+ Add missed claim” (adds a new row with status = "added"), “← Previous”, “Accept all →”, “Save & Next →”.
  • Sidebar: progress counters + a reminder of the shortcuts.

Keyboard shortcuts (fast mode)

Key Action
n Save & Next
p Previous
a Accept all visible
+ Add missed claim
1–9 Toggle Accept on claim n

With shortcuts you can review about 2 abstracts per minute when Gemma 4 got the claims right (just a + n). Complex claims take about 30 s to edit.

Tab 2 – Stats

  • Table per abstract: n_draft · n_accepted · n_edited · n_added · n_rejected.
  • Bar plot of canonical-vocabulary coverage across accepted claims – useful to see whether the corpus covers all 22 concepts or has gaps.

Tab 3 – Export

Clicking “Validate & export” runs the logic of llm_annotation_export():

  1. Drops every rejected claim.
  2. Drops claims still at status = "draft" (the reviewer did not touch them – we exclude them conservatively).
  3. Removes the internal status field.
  4. Validates vocabulary + polarity + confidence.
  5. Writes reviewed_gold_v2_final.jsonl.

Step 4 – Re-run the benchmark

With the expanded gold standard, point the benchmark runner at the new file:

# Edit data-raw/llm_benchmark_run.R line 22:
# gold_path <- "inst/extdata/cerrado_gold_standard_v2_final.jsonl"

source("data-raw/llm_benchmark_run.R")

The P/R/F1/κ figures are then publication-grade.

Annotation good practice

Suggested annotation criteria (for internal consistency within your gold standard):

  1. Be conservative with confidence. 0.90+ only when the text cites a controlled study or a quantified magnitude; 0.70 for claims well supported by mechanism but without a number; 0.50 for suggestive ones.
  2. Canonical vocabulary first. If the text mentions “tree cover”, use vegetation. If it mentions “annual rainfall”, use mean_annual_precipitation. Consistency matters more than literal fidelity.
  3. Polarity is a sign, not a magnitude. “Reduces SOC” → -. “Increases”, “raises”, “accelerates” → +. Conditional claims (“reduces if > 2 AU/ha”) are still - in the gold standard; the confidence may drop.
  4. One claim per direct mechanism. If the text says “rainfall → NPP → SOC”, record two claims (precip → vegetation, vegetation → soc), not one indirect claim.
  5. Rationale = one line. A fragment of the text that supports the claim. Useful for later audits and for training the next iteration of the prompt.

Further features

Production corpus fetcher 

# Needs the network. Free. About 40 s for 6 queries x 60 results.
Sys.setenv(EDAPHOS_CORPUS_MAILTO = "rodrigues.machado.hugo@gmail.com")
source("data-raw/cerrado_corpus_v2_fetch.R")
# -> inst/extdata/cerrado_corpus_openalex_v2.jsonl  (~150 abstracts)

Live DAG preview

In the app, the DAG tab renders a DiagrammeR::grViz() of the graph aggregated from every claim whose status is accepted | edited | added:

  • A min_support slider filters edges by number of occurrences (useful when the corpus is large and you want only edges confirmed by several abstracts).
  • Edge colours: green = +, red = −.
  • Edge width ∝ mean confidence.
  • A label toggle shows the structure without names (useful for paper figures).

Dark mode

A toggle in the sidebar (uses bslib::input_dark_mode()). It follows the operating system’s preference.

Publishing on Zenodo

The Publish tab packages everything into a Zenodo-ready directory:

# The same, programmatically
edaphos::llm_annotation_to_zenodo(
  reviewed_path = "reviewed_gold_v2_final.jsonl",
  output_dir    = "~/Desktop/zenodo_cerrado_kg",
  title         = "Cerrado Pedogenesis KG (edaphos, v2, 2026-04)",
  authors       = data.frame(
    family_name = "Rodrigues", given_name = "Hugo",
    orcid       = "0000-0002-8070-8126",
    affiliation = "Your institution"
  ),
  keywords      = c("Cerrado", "pedometrics", "soil organic carbon",
                     "knowledge graph", "causal inference"),
  license       = "CC-BY-4.0",
  zip           = TRUE
)

Contents of the bundle:

File Role
gold_standard.jsonl Clean gold standard (draft/rejected removed)
kg.ttl Graph serialised as RDF 1.1 Turtle (each claim becomes a reified rdf:Statement with predicates eda:polarity, eda:confidence, dct:source)
metadata.json DataCite-compatible; ready for the Zenodo REST API
README.md Description, counts, provenance, citation

Upload by hand at https://zenodo.org/deposit/new, paste the fields of metadata.json into the form, publish, and record the minted DOI in your paper’s CITATION.cff.

Next steps

These are open items, named rather than numbered.

  • Full production run: fetcher → Gemma 4 → human annotation → Zenodo deposit with a real DOI. About three hours of a pedologist’s time plus about 40 minutes of machine time.
  • Weighted voting by default: make weighted voting (Gemma + Claude) the default of causal_llm_ingest_abstract_voted(), calibrated by the backend-vs-gold κ derived from the benchmark.

References

  • Landis, J. R. & Koch, G. G. (1977). “The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data.” Biometrics 33, 159-174.
